name: Hair growth laser comb (HairMax)

card.summary: A handheld FDA-cleared low-level laser comb that parts the hair and delivers red light to the scalp to thicken thinning hair.
card.note: Used on a regular schedule; trial results are for pattern hair loss.

quick.overview:
The HairMax LaserComb is a handheld device with comb teeth that part the hair so that red laser light reaches the scalp. It is used by people with pattern hair loss who want denser, thicker-looking hair, and is one of the few non-drug options the FDA has cleared for androgenetic alopecia.

Sham-controlled trials of the comb reported increases in terminal hair density over 26 weeks, and systematic reviews of low-level laser therapy generally report improvements in hair count. Effects are measured as density and thickness, and patient satisfaction was reported as positive but less pronounced than the objective measures.
quick.how: Users pass the comb slowly over the scalp for several minutes, a few times a week, often alongside minoxidil or finasteride. The 2014 trials used treatment three times a week for 26 weeks [2]. Changes build over months.
quick.risks: Trials and reviews report the devices as well tolerated, with mild scalp reactions occasionally noted. Results vary between people, and benefit depends on continued use. A dermatologist can confirm the cause of hair loss before a device is tried.

lead: The HairMax LaserComb is a handheld low-level laser therapy (LLLT) device made by Lexington International. It is a Class 3R laser emitting nine beams at 655 nm, with comb teeth aligned to the beams so that hair is parted and light reaches the scalp [1]. The FDA has cleared it for androgenetic alopecia, making it, with minoxidil and finasteride, one of the treatments the FDA recognises for male pattern hair loss [3].

People use it to thicken thin areas and slow visible hair loss, appearing as fuller hair. In a sham-controlled, double-blind trial of men with Norwood-Hamilton IIa-V hair loss, the device was assessed over 26 weeks [1]. A later multicentre trial of 128 men and 141 women compared three comb models to sham devices at three sessions a week for 26 weeks, measuring terminal hair density [2].

A systematic review of 11 LLLT studies covering 680 patients found 9 of 11 reporting statistically significant improvements in hair density or count [4], and a 2017 meta-analysis found that LLLT in men was superior to placebo, alongside minoxidil and finasteride [5]. Reviews note that patient-reported satisfaction was positive but less marked than objective results [4].

chain: Red laser light delivered to the scalp through the comb
More and thicker terminal hairs over months
angle.text: The comb is used to build visible density in thinning areas of the scalp. Results appear gradually over several months of regular sessions and are measured as hair count and thickness.

infobox: Male and female pattern hair loss

paras: The comb teeth are matched to the beams so hair does not block the light [1]. The proposed mechanism is photobiomodulation, in which low-level light is thought to stimulate follicle cells; reviews describe LLLT as proposed to stimulate regrowth in androgenetic alopecia [4].

On forums the comb is discussed as one tool among hair-loss options. Hair-loss threads typically refer to the finasteride, minoxidil and laser 'big 3' alongside other topicals. Lifters on T Nation have also discussed hair-loss management alongside testosterone therapy [6].

A 26-week sham-controlled, double-blind trial tested the HairMax LaserComb in men with androgenetic alopecia [1]. A multicentre trial in 128 men and 141 women randomised participants to one of three comb models or sham, and measured terminal hair density at 16 and 26 weeks [2]. A systematic review of 11 studies in 680 patients reported significant hair count or density improvements in 9 of 11 [4]. A 2017 meta-analysis of randomised trials found laser therapy in men superior to placebo [5]. Animal work has examined laser combs in mouse alopecia areata and rat chemotherapy-induced alopecia models [7][8]. Wikipedia notes that earlier reviews (2012-2015) found tentative or mixed evidence and that a 2019 meta-analysis found increased density across device types [9].
